# Translator’s Preface.

The value of the work, the translation of which I hereby present to the public, has been judged by my venerable friend in the following letter, in my view, so impartially, truthfully, and accurately that nothing remains for me to add. I also have little to say regarding my own translation. I have endeavored to grasp the author’s <note>The original German uses the feminine "Verfasserin," indicating the author of the source text is a woman.</note> meaning correctly and to express it faithfully and understandably. I have spent no more effort on the style of writing than was necessary to make the work readable. Had I wished to apply a modern coloring <note>original: "Kolorit"; refers to the stylistic tone or "flavor" of the writing</note>, as the taste of our belletristic <term>belletristic: relating to "belles-lettres," a category of writing focused on aesthetic elegance rather than scientific or philosophical depth</term> age demands, the unique character of the original would have been lost; I preferred to preserve this character rather than to artificially embellish it for the sake of pleasing readers who would never find any taste for the subject matter itself, even under the most beautiful veneer. This work can perhaps only find acceptance among people who are not offended by any form simply because it is a form, but who everywhere

What is significantly known regarding the life of Schurman, beyond what she herself relates of it in this work, is as follows.

She was born in the year 1607, on the 5th of November, in Cologne, and descended from a noble and wealthy Dutch family, which, along with many others, had fled to Germany to escape the cruelty of the Duke of Alba <note>Fernando Álvarez de Toledo, the Duke of Alba, was a Spanish governor known for his harsh suppression of Protestants in the Netherlands.</note> against the Protestants. VII

The reputation she soon acquired through her extensive erudition and her admirable skill in arts and sciences gained her the esteem and acquaintance of a multitude of both princely persons and the most famous scholars in various countries. Everyone considered her correspondence an honor and sought to get to know her personally, which is why she was overwhelmed with visits, even from the most distinguished individuals.

Queen Christina of Sweden, to whom she had previously sent a poem in her praise along with a work of art by her own hand, visited her in 1651 after her abdication during a journey to Holland. She found occasion to admire both her erudition and her artistic skill simultaneously; for she cornered several Jesuits <note>Members of the Society of Jesus, known for their rigorous education and debating skills</note> who accompanied the Queen and had engaged her in theological disputes in the Queen's presence. Upon her departure, she presented the Queen with her portrait, which she had sketched during the visit. — 

At Utrecht, she had her own separate place in the university lecture hall, where she often attended public disputations <note>Formal academic debates conducted in Latin</note> and is said to have occasionally joined in the disputation herself. — 

What remains of her scholarly works from this period can be found in her by no means rare <term>Opuscula</term> <note>original: "Opusculis"; small or minor works, often a collection of shorter essays or poems</note>, where one also finds the <term>Eulogies</term> <note>original: "Elogia"; formal speeches or writings praising a person</note> of the most famous scholars,

XIII

To everyone, it felt as if they were listening to an Apollo speaking from the tripod <note>A reference to the Pythia, the priestess of the Oracle of Delphi, who sat on a tripod to deliver divine prophecies.</note>. Following this, a conversation arose between him and our Superintendent <term>Superintendent: a high-ranking administrative official in the Lutheran church</term> regarding the carnal desires of man, which tend to plague and carry away our souls so greatly. They disputed over this for an entire hour with great heat, without settling anything, until finally Princess Elisabeth <note>Elisabeth of the Palatinate (1618–1680), a philosopher and abbess of Herford who famously corresponded with Descartes.</note>, weary of the shouting, put an end to the quarrel and invited them both to her quarters for the afternoon. Here, much was disputed again, and Labadie was reproached for having forbidden women—through exaggerated severity and abstinence—all jewelry, gemstones, and other feminine finery. It was argued that he had confused the poor souls of the weaker sex, who were so easily led astray and seduced, through a fearful and anxious piety. Indeed, in the early Church, there had been women who, adorned with gold and purple, came into the temples and graced the Christian assemblies with their piety; and now, should those not be able to be pious or holy who had a few gemstones hanging around their necks, or wore a ring on their finger, or whose foreheads were adorned with artfully braided locks of hair? For these women could surely bring just as pure and chaste a heart into the temples as

of the goods of heaven, and was declared innocent and holy. All other men, he claimed, still lay in their sins, defiling themselves daily through vice and following the ruinous allurements of the world. His followers, on the other hand, never soiled their feet with the dust of the earth, nor did their minds ever dwell in this lowly mire in which we miserable ones still wallow; instead, they already sat among the angels of heaven and at the throne of God, looking down from there with contempt and mockery upon the misery of poor mortals. Furthermore, how absurd and foolish it is that he dares to assert he knows which man is holy and reborn <note>The concept of being "born again" or "regenerate" was a central point of contention in 17th-century Pietism</note>, since the human soul is so fertile in deceit, so rich in malice and hypocrisy, that it often hides the greatest wickedness under the cloak of the strictest piety. This judgment truly belongs to God alone, who is present in the depths of the soul and knows its most secret thoughts; but men err grossly when, deluded by false madness or puffed up by ambition, they presumptuously wish to decide on things that they can neither see with their eyes nor securely investigate through their reason.

# Letter
## from the Author of the Annotations

**H**ere, my dear friend, you have everything that I have seen fit to note regarding the original and your translation of the *Eukleria* <note>The title *Eukleria* is derived from Greek, meaning "the choosing of the better part," referencing the biblical story of Mary and Martha.</note> by our Lady van Schurman. Make use of it as best you can.
      A few words about the impression the book has made on me. In your announcement, you approve of the laudable judgment which Mr. Wieland <note>Christoph Martin Wieland (1733–1813), a highly influential German Enlightenment poet and writer.</note> passed a few years ago \*) on its nature and value. How far the public will agree with this does not concern me. For my part, I would wish this *Eukleria* to be viewed from two sides: first, as the history of an innocent, lovely soul; and second, as a fruit of religion, which recommends itself at the very least through truth and the fervor <note>original: "Inbrunft"</note> of the heart. In the former respect, the historical part of this work has much that is entertaining and some quite special charms; in the latter, however, much might be found therein which one would nowadays prefer not to read. As a fruit of—

# Page XXII

In terms of religion, the work does not entirely correspond to the idea that I had previously formed of it. Precisely from <term>Schurman</term> <note>Anna Maria van Schurman (1607–1678), a famous Dutch scholar and artist who later joined the Labadist pietist sect.</note> I expected a fruit—I will not say more beautiful—but certainly more unique. An image of religion that would resemble a Raphael Madonna rather than a Dutch saint.

But what entitled her, you will ask, to that high idea? In part, the essays which Mr. Wieland <note>Christoph Martin Wieland, a major Enlightenment writer and contemporary of the author.</note> counts among her learned "night-wanderings." I do not know in what sense—whether considered as essays in general, or because they come from a woman, or finally in the relation of human art to the higher destiny and dignity of our nature. In this latter sense, she herself calls her entire previous life a dream, indeed a shadow of a dream, <note>original: "Somnium et umbram Somnii"</note>. I understand quite well that to the eye of a higher spectator, all the swarm and bustle on our globe could and must reveal itself as a dream and child's play; and indeed in a truer sense than according to the hypothesis of some philosophers, where the entire beauty of the visible world consists in mere deceptions of the senses. If one, however, considers those small writings merely as specimens of art, they might, from this perspective, far outweigh the <term>Eukleria</term> <note>Schurman's autobiographical work "Eukleria" (1673), written to justify her choice of a quietist, religious life over her former fame.</note>. # Preface

...a genius that, if it did not thwart itself, at least imitated the vanity of literary life; yet they also provide, at the same time, the image of a soul that invented, formed, and imitated in every kind of writing and language, just as it did in every art: a soul that rejoiced in innocence over every flower of creation as well as every play of the human spirit. Throughout these works, there is a sensitive delicacy in the choice of thought and expression, of which the *Eukleria* <note>The *Eukleria* (from the Greek for "good portion" or "well-being") is the title of Anna Maria van Schurman's spiritual autobiography, published in 1673.</note> shows far fewer traces.

Now, I am well aware that neither the merit of a saint, nor the value of a writing intended to be a "good portion," consists in fine, select thoughts and beautiful language. The former lies rather in something for which the world has no name, no standard, and no comparisons: and the latter in a little-known, deeply hidden, but very living spirit, which bears the imperishable seal of a higher descent and tastes a celestial world. Something of this kind truly reveals itself in our *Eukleria*: and to deny it would betray no less blindness than injustice. Despite all this, however, I still miss that consistent simplicity, calm, and sublimity, which distinguishes itself not only from the inclination toward commonplace <term>theological deductions</term> <note>Logical arguments derived from scripture, often criticized by mystics for being too intellectual and lacking heart.</note>, but also from the common fruits of <term>Pietism</term> <note>A movement within Lutheranism that emphasized individual piety and the "religion of the heart" over formal dogma.</note> and <term>Separatism</term> <note>The practice of withdrawing from established churches to form independent religious communities.</note>, just as the higher spirit of art and ideas—

Perhaps Schurman <note>Anna Maria van Schurman (1607–1678), a famous Dutch scholar and artist who later joined a radical pietist sect</note> would have achieved something similar if she had remained in a state of calm resignation in God and without connection to the <term>Labadists<note>Followers of Jean de Labadie, a communal pietist sect that sought to return to the purity of the early Christian church</note></term>. # XXV

The contradiction seems to vanish. A great many people must consider her step toward Labadism <note>A radical pietist movement founded by Jean de Labadie, emphasizing communal living and internal piety.</note> to be very violent and unnatural; I believe, however, that it is to be sought in a natural progression of her soul; in a need of her heart, which she sought to satisfy in this way as best as she could at that time. As soon as this urge of the heart—this "feeling for God" <note>original: "Gottesgefühl"</note> which seemed innate to her—became powerful within her, she reached for the "One Thing Needful" <note>A reference to Luke 10:42, a common pietist trope regarding the priority of spiritual life over worldly affairs.</note> and considered union with a few separated individuals, who made this same "chosen portion" the goal of their lives, to be absolutely essential. This perceived necessity was, in my opinion, a delusion; to her, however, it was a matter of conscience, which she believed she must necessarily follow. In herself, she could have lived according to that chosen portion even without Labadism, and would have remained at peace in doing so. But since she considered a communion with the true Church to be necessary, and believed this was to be found solely and exclusively in the "little flock" <note>original: "Häuflein"</note> of the Labadists, the transition to them caused her not the slightest hesitation. She therefore subjected herself to all those disturbances, eternal tribulations, and persecutions which she experienced in the final years of her life all the more willingly, because she thereby gained in Christian tolerance, humility, self-conquest, and steadfastness in suffering and hope; but she was also, by chance, led toward things which

What an extraordinary impression Labadie <note>Jean de Labadie (1610–1674), a French mystic and former Jesuit who founded the Pietist communal sect known as the Labadists.</note> made upon her can already be seen from the reverence with which she speaks of him everywhere. It was primarily sermons or practical lectures through which he exerted such power over her. She believed she found in his speeches that spirit of truth which seemed to her the surest proof of a faithful and proven servant of God and a true successor of the Apostles, as she constantly calls him. Therefore, she did everything possible to be near him, allowed herself to be deterred by no difficulties, clung—so to speak—with her entire happiness to his person, followed his voice like a faithful sheep, and received his words like the speech of an angel of God. This almost oracle-like veneration of a man who, through his practical talents and the way in which he applied them, differed not a little from the clergy of his time—this veneration, I say, explains a large part of our book. Many weaknesses of her later way of thinking, incorrect interpretations and applications of certain scriptural passages, and certain one-sided, often too harsh judgments about the ordinary system of things, flowed entirely from this source.

# XXVII

See here, dear friend, these are my thoughts on the *Eukleria* <note>The title of Anna Maria van Schurman’s autobiography, meaning "Choosing the Good Portion."</note> taken as a whole. Now, a little more regarding its specific content. I have already remarked previously that the historical content of this work is by far its most excellent feature. What she says in the first part (Chapters 1 and 2) concerning the history of her education and youthful years, her natural talents of mind and heart, her scholarly studies, and so forth, will be read by no one without pleasure. The subsequent evaluation (Chapter 3) of the sciences according to their value and influence on the true knowledge and happiness of mankind will already please much less. She devalues these sources of knowledge almost entirely, despite how much she had previously esteemed them and even boasted of them herself. She does this, however, not with the satirical bitterness of a Cornelius Agrippa in his *On the Vanity of the Sciences* <note>original: "de Vanitate scientiarum"; a famous 16th-century skeptical work by Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa.</note>; rather, she considers them merely according to her own experience, because she did not find in them that for which her soul had thirsted since childhood. She believes, therefore, that these celebrated sources of knowledge have much of the nature of those dead and silent idols about them, which give the least answer precisely when one has the greatest need of their help. In general, this "maidenly critique" must be viewed merely in relation to religion—specifically that degree of religion which she alone considered authentic at that time. According to her perspective <term>Augenmaaß: literally "measure of the eye," referring to her subjective judgment or point of view</term> at that time, she could not have judged otherwise. However little she

I must marvel at how the amiable Schurman <note>Anna Maria van Schurman (1607–1678), a famous Dutch scholar and the first woman to attend a university, who later joined the radical Labadist sect.</note> could, I will not say digest, but rather defend and praise such harsh things with an unusual vehemence. This entire misunderstood chatter, like much else, is quite unworthy of her. A modest maiden should have left such dogmas to harsher men, even if they belonged to the doctrinal system of the church to which she generally professed her allegiance. Following this (Chapter 5) is an equally useless polemic against Madame Bourignon <note>Antoinette Bourignon (1616–1680), a Flemish mystic and rival to the Labadist movement.</note> regarding the satisfaction of Christ <term>Satisfaction of Christ: the theological doctrine that Christ's suffering paid the debt for human sin.</term> and predestination. The only good thing therein is that she is modest enough to confess that she cannot and will not boast of any abrupt, immediate revelations from God. In the 6th Chapter, she defends herself against the polemic of a certain Bachelor of Theology, Johann Gabriel Drechsler, who had challenged the first part of her *Eukleria* <note>Schurman's autobiographical defense of her choice to join the Labadists, titled "Eukleria, or Choosing the Better Part."</note>, especially her judgments on the value and utility of the sciences; on this occasion, she speaks once more about this matter, and at the same time about the concept of true Christianity. Finally, the conclusion (Chapter 7) consists of some reports regarding a certain dispute that had broken out between Gisbertus Voetius <note>A prominent Dutch Reformed theologian and former mentor to Schurman.</note>, one of her former friends and admirers, and the Labadist community. From two appended letters concerning her death, one sees that she died just a few days after completing the second part of the *Eukleria*.

<meta>The previous page concluded with a discussion of historical texts; this page serves as the concluding reflection of the letter, transitioning from historical critique to a philosophical hope for religious harmony.</meta>

I close my tedious letter with the observation that this book, like a thousand others, confirms the historical truth of how much religion has been misused in all ages by the so-called defenders of the "good cause." God gave religion for the sake of peace. And indeed, nothing should be more powerful than religion to unite the hearts of mankind in love; instead, however, through no fault of its own, it has had to become an object of strife and persecution throughout all time. Our times are becoming milder, for which Providence <note>The protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power.</note> cannot be praised enough. To be sure, what is now called tolerance <note>original: "Toleranz"</note> can degenerate into complete indifference toward genuine biblical religion; but it can also be a tool in the hand of God, through which a faith in religion is gradually brought about that is neither sectarianism <note>original: "Sectirerei"</note> nor forgetfulness of God. And this is what every sincere worshiper of God and friend of truth must wish for with all their heart.

->Farewell! Yours, etc. etc.<-

# The Power of Divine Truth

The mighty power of its truth and holiness is felt more vividly than anything that can act upon them through the external senses—much like a coal cast into their hearts from the altar by an angel <note>A reference to Isaiah 6:6, symbolizing purification and divine commissioning</note>. And this is no wonder, since every thing possesses all the more reality, and acts all the more powerfully, the more spiritual it is. Meanwhile, if we seek something fully demonstrative, or an irrefutable proof of the divinity and efficacy of this doctrine, we must certainly not rely too heavily on those sudden or even fiery stirrings which not infrequently arise through the hearing of the Word—as our Savior teaches in Matthew 13 <note>The Parable of the Sower, specifically the seeds falling on rocky ground</note> and his Apostle in Hebrews 6—but which can entirely disappear over time and through adversities, as is the case with a transitory faith.

However, we can also sincerely and truthfully boast in the Lord of the most reliable and peculiar effect of this doctrine: that which the Psalmist ascribes to the doctrine of Jehovah <note>original: "Jehovahs"</note>, namely, that it renews the spirit. Of this we truly have among us just as many proofs and witnesses as there are members of our—

17) It is indeed a great fortune to be born to and raised by parents who themselves know religion and love it from the heart. The fruits of this are visible in such children at a very early age. One can manage them much better in every way, even in all other matters. Anyone with some experience in churches and schools will have easily noticed all of this. From this perspective, too, religion cannot be valued enough. Where it is the soul of a house, it is also the guardian spirit of every pupil. Otherwise, instruction based merely on textbooks means very little.

<margin>25) If one wanted to relate everything so strictly to religion, much would lose its value which God nevertheless bestowed upon mankind not without purpose. Aristotle calls man the most imitative of all creatures. Our author is a remarkable example of this kind. Her art of imitation extended with equal perfection to the works of the fingers as to those of the mind. She therefore also wrote every language, even the most difficult, according to its own peculiar spirit. Her Latin, Greek, Hebrew, French, etc., essays are examples of this.</margin>

The features of the miniature portrait were not only very similar to my own, but because of the vivid brilliance and the curvature of the eyeball, it seemed—if one moved the case quickly—as if the eyes of the image moved of their own accord. The waxen hair was attached to the head only by its finest tips, so that it hung down in free-flowing and seemingly natural curls. The most difficult task of all, however, was the eyelashes, which my stubborn diligence had set with indescribably fine little hairs; and (to add this one last detail of its vain finery) the small pearls around the neck were, through a new invention of my own making, so perfectly indistinguishable from natural ones that people would hardly believe me when I asserted the contrary. Thus, to prove the truth, I was once obliged—at the request of the ingenious <note>The word "sinnreich" here implies both cleverness and an appreciation for the arts.</note> Countess of Nassau—to pierce one of them through with a small needle.

But what fruit did I gather from this in the end, other than that I recklessly purchased for myself, with the loss of such precious time, the regret which its fall and destruction soon after brought upon me? One might well laugh at this madness of the human soul in philosophers who mistake their sublime thoughts and high-sounding words regarding the contempt for external things—in which Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – AD 65), a Stoic philosopher known for advocating indifference to worldly fortune</note> with his paradoxes formerly pleased me quite particularly—for the true state and actual constitution of their soul. 

But should one laugh or weep? when one sees, as is only too often the case, how alleged Christians in their supposed spiritual and religious life seize upon beautifully devised matters—or things they have confessed with their mouths and carry around in their heads or in their speeches, especially concerning the denial of external things and the practice of faith, hope, and love—as if these were real truths and virtues which they dream of actually possessing, and thus settle into this imagined bliss. Whereby many, like the philosophers of old of whom Paul speaks (Romans 1:21 <note>original: "Röm. 1, 21." The verse describes those who became vain in their thinking and whose foolish hearts were darkened</note>), have become vain in their thinking, and, while considering themselves wise, have become fools.

I shall pass over other matters of this kind, because I have begun to lose my affection for such things and my memory of them, just as the divine image of the life of Christ presented itself to my soul. Since I now found this alone worthy of imitation, and yet could not always maintain it clearly and steadily enough in my mind, I occupied myself with composing a written sketch of it, as perfect as possible, for my own benefit and that of others. The excellent little book by Thomas à Kempis <note>Thomas à Kempis (c. 1380–1471) was a German-Dutch canon regular and author of "The Imitation of Christ," one of the most influential Christian devotional books.</note>, *On the Imitation of Christ*, had always pleased me greatly; however, I did not find everything in it that the title promised, nor what I flattered myself I might be able to achieve to some extent. But, to confess the truth, I have never been able to satisfy myself with this work, partly because the radiance of this divine subject often dazzled my spirit and eyes, and partly because I saw that I was painting the sun with only a piece of charcoal. I found that the best and truest image of the life of Christ was the life of Christians, though I regret that it is so rarely to be found in our times. But when I subsequently perceived its most vivid features in the leaders of our congregation <note>original: "Gemeine," referring here to the Moravian Brethren or a similar pietistic community</note>, I believed I had to exchange all works of art for these living models. As I expressed this earnest intention of mine in a letter to a certain distinguished patron of the sciences and arts (who desired to know my judgment on certain excellent paintings) shortly before my departure from Utrecht <note>A prominent city in the Netherlands, known for its university and as a center of religious thought.</note>,

The arts granted to me served to draw me away from childhood games and other pastimes; but now I add that I was also quite well-protected against the useless and worldly societies that awaited me in my more mature years. This was due partly to my father’s precise instruction in the duties of piety <note>German: Frömmigkeit; a central concept in 17th-century devotion emphasizing personal holiness and lived faith</note> (whereby I must also not forget my dear mother’s care), and partly through his frequent exhortations, with which he warned me against the contagion of the times and association with worldly-minded people. And so that I might not unexpectedly become entangled in the snares of this world, he admonished me especially—most strongly and zealously while on his deathbed—that I should guard myself against the highly corrupt and indissoluble bond of a worldly marriage (as most are nowadays). I never afterwards forgot this paternal advice when the world sought to chain me to itself in this manner through various means and ways.

Next to these are physics, metaphysics, history, etc., as well as linguistics, especially Hebrew and Greek; all of which can be helpful to us for a easier and more perfect understanding of the Holy Scriptures (not to mention other books)."

One sees from this that I did indeed subordinate everything to the study of theology as the most noble pursuit; however, this subordination extended almost into infinity, and thus marked out a monstrously long path toward the goal of pure theology. 45) Not as if a Christian, because he is a Christian, must necessarily also be the best naturalist (in a scientific sense), but because he, above others, is in a position to look upon nature with the right eyes, and brings with him those auxiliary and mediating concepts which serve above all things for a correct explanation of the same. Certainly, a **Nieuwentyt** <note>Bernard Nieuwentyt (1654–1718), a Dutch philosopher and mathematician who argued that the complexity of nature proved the existence of God</note> must look at nature with different eyes than a mere pagan. The former already knows its Author; the latter is only just seeking Him out, and generally does not yet know if or to what extent nature has one. Here, moreover, we are speaking of the true and great sense of religion, which is at the same time the true and great sense of nature. In this way, **Pascal** <note>Blaise Pascal (1623–1662), French mathematician and theologian</note> also says in his *Thoughts* <note>original: "Pensées"</note> that the Bible is the best **codex** <term>codex: a manuscript book; here used to mean a foundational reference or guidebook</term> for the explanation of nature, although it does not teach how animals and plants must be anatomized.

The means which moral philosophy <term>Moralphilosophie; the study of ethics and human conduct</term> demands for the attainment of that ultimate goal are no less vain than they are manifold and diverse. For if we consider the Peripatetic <note>The school of philosophy founded by Aristotle, known for teaching while walking about</note> school from this perspective, how far and wide does it stretch—as Seneca says—the targets of its happiness! For it requires, namely, for the exercise of the virtues, or for the perfection and authenticity of bliss, all external goods as well: freedom, health, wealth, dignity, delights, and so forth, along with the lack and absence of all evil. The Stoics <note>A school of philosophy that taught that virtue is the only good and that we should remain indifferent to external circumstances</note> seem, of course, to be much more magnanimous and noble-minded here, since they claim that virtue alone is content with itself and sufficient for itself, and that in the presence of such a great light—namely, virtue—a tiny spark <note>Referring to external comforts or worldly goods</note> does not come into consideration at all; indeed, that the wise man is happy even under the greatest tortures. This, one might believe, comes very close to the teachings of Christianity, which assure us that for those who love God, all things work together for the best; and that even persecution, disgrace, and poverty make Christians blessed. But—and this applies to both, the Peripatetics as well as the Stoics—what could be more ruinous and more contrary to the Christian life than to find peace in human virtue, and to make it, instead of God, one's highest good? And, even if one otherwise holds worthy concepts of God, to seek in this knowledge more one's own honor than the honor of God, and everything...

# Fourth Section.

## Concerning Christian Theology, the Law, and the Gospel.

### As well as concerning my former piety and its practices, especially the Sabbath and its former almost Jewish observance.

From what has preceded, one can see clearly enough that I spent much time and effort on superfluous things and observed no moderation in the human sciences <note>The author refers to secular academic studies like philosophy or philology</note>. I come now, therefore, to the truths of Reformed Theology <note>The branch of Protestantism following the traditions of Calvin and Zwingli</note> and the exercises of piety, to which I subordinated everything else. In this regard, I was considered very fortunate by many, because I seemed to have progressed so far in these matters that I had no need to go further straight ahead, but only to walk in a circle, as it were, to keep everything constantly new and alive for myself. And indeed, I applied myself not only to theoretical theology and the theory of practical theology, but also to the exercise of the practical with a sincere heart according to the small measure of my grace. But just as in other things, objects and concepts are often very different from one another; so I am also learning now through daily experience that between those things grasped with the intellect—painted, as it were, in the soul—and those also held with a certain love in the hear—

# On Religious Observance

...piety, but this clearly smacks of Judaism <note>The author is referring to the strict, legalistic observance of the Sabbath, which he associates with Jewish tradition</note>. A people freed from all those observations and distinctions of days and places, and other external customs, and consecrated in soul and body to Christ (as they are purchased and redeemed by His blood). One of the most distinguished theologians from Utrecht <note>Likely a reference to the school of Gisbertus Voetius or his contemporaries involved in the 17th-century Dutch Sabbath controversies</note> insisted most strongly on the following argument, derived from the doctrine of classifications: Since the Law of God in the Old Testament was threefold—the political, the ceremonial, and the moral, or the Law of Love, the latter of which contained the Ten Commandments written by the hand of God himself on stone and durable tablets to last forever—it would be highly absurd if someone wanted to include something ceremonial within this Law of Love, or the moral law. This would be no less absurd than if someone were to divide living creatures into rational and irrational, and then divide the rational ones again into rational and irrational.

But who does not see how many disputed points are here taken for granted? For who will prove that the law of stone, which Divine Providence allowed to perish even before the arrival of Christ, was intended to last forever? And who can reasonably exclude the Law of Love from the political law? And can one not assert with greater right that the Ten Commandments, in which God proclaimed His will to the Jewish people in such an extraordinary and solemn manner, are (as I said before) a brief summary of all other Jewish laws, which at that time had to be kept with equal obedience? I wish to add a few brief remarks here as an appendix regarding a certain misuse of sermons—one which people commonly mistake for the best possible use of them. Specifically, there is a belief that one must not only impress them upon the memory with great diligence, but also, in order to assist the memory, commit them to paper or have them printed, so that by reading them repeatedly afterward, one might derive greater benefit from them. I was formerly of this same opinion, but I find now that this procedure is very literal <note>The author uses "literal" here in the sense of "clinging to the dead letter" rather than the living spirit.</note> and smacks of Judaism. For the Jews were commanded to make their phylacteries <note>original: "Denkzettel." These are small leather boxes containing scripture texts worn by observant Jews; the author uses this as a metaphor for externalizing faith.</note> wide because they did not possess the Spirit which Christ promised to his disciples—the Spirit who, in His own time and according to the requirements of the circumstances, would remind them of His words.

The best way to hear the Word of God, however—as I am convinced by experience—is to quietly and faithfully cherish that which has been heard and captured within the heart. One should not seek its application with great effort at certain fixed times, but rather expect it humbly from divine grace and providence. There is likely no one who is not pleased by the saying of Augustine: *The pulpit is on earth, but the Teacher is in heaven* <note>original Latin: "Cathedra in terris, Doctor in caelis." A common Pietist reference to the "Internal Teacher" or Holy Spirit.</note>; nor is there anyone who has not often had the well-known saying of the Apostle on their lips: We are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:5.</note>. # On the Marks of the True Church

The verses which are attributed to the visible Church on earth—partly by Christ himself, partly by his Apostles and other writers guided by the Holy Spirit—I shall pass over. This is because they have been fully explained by our venerable leader, Jean de Labadie <note>Jean de Labadie (1610–1674) was a French mystic and reformer who founded the Labadist pietist movement, seeking a "pure" church of the reborn.</note>, among many other arguments, in a specific work composed in Geneva and published in Amsterdam under the title: *Le Discernement d'une veritable Eglise*, that is, *The Discernment of a True Church* <note>original: "Le Discernement d'une veritable Eglise"</note>.

I know that some object to this, claiming that these glorious names are only attributed to the Church in consideration of its "better part," even though the number of the unregenerate <term>unregenerate: those who have not experienced a spiritual rebirth or conversion</term> far exceeds that of the reborn. They argue that almost the same titles of honor—such as **People of God**, **Heritage of God**, indeed the **Holy People**, and the **Royal Priesthood**—were attributed to the Jews of the Old Testament, of whom clearly only a very small portion consisted of true believers.

To this, however, I answer firstly: that such a thing cannot take place in a "body" or a collective whole, such as the body of the Church is. For who can with any justification call a heap of chaff a "heap of wheat," even if a few grains of wheat are mixed in among it? Or who will honor a herd of swine with the name "herd of sheep," even if he sees a sheep wandering here and there among them? Who will say that a King's army is "faithful" to him if it consists of rebels, among whom—

# On the Practice of Christian Fellowship

One must be careful in the practice of Christian fellowship, since the Apostle says that every one shall give account of himself to God, and shall bear his own burden. <note>References to Romans 14:12 and Galatians 6:5.</note> For this reason, there have been people who boasted that they would not be troubled at all, even if the Devil himself stood by their side during the celebration of the Holy Supper. I must confess that a shudder came over me at these words; especially when I heard that even by people who stand in the reputation of piety, the sayings of Holy Scripture were so distorted to the greatest insult of true godliness. 

But let them see to it themselves, that they do not prepare too easy an entrance for that "roaring lion, who walketh about, seeking whom he may devour," <note>A reference to 1 Peter 5:8.</note> into such assemblies where they—in a solemn manner, as it were—allow incarnate devils (that is, worldly-minded and unregenerate people, who harm more imperceptibly and thus more dangerously) to take their place. Meanwhile, if they believe their Catechism, they bring the wrath of God upon the entire congregation by admitting the ungodly to the <term>seals of the New Covenant</term> <note>A theological term for the Sacraments, specifically Baptism and the Lord's Supper, viewed as visible signs of God's promises.</note>.

While Labadie <note>Jean de Labadie (1610–1674), a former Jesuit turned Pietist leader</note> lived, he was the soul of the society; after his death, everything declined more and more, until finally the entire *little church* <note>original: "Ecclesiola," a term for a small, devout circle within a larger church</note> was extinguished.

63) From which she and her little church <note>Referring to the small community of followers or "house church"</note> were to suffer much in the future. This **theological hatred** <note>original: "odium theologicum"</note> has produced such sad effects at all times, even though peace is a primary principle of Christianity. If one wishes to look at the majority, one could rightly call it "synodal hatred" <note>original: "Synodalhaß"</note>. This also included their entire consistory <note>a governing body of a local church</note>, which consisted for the most part of respected and elderly citizens of the city of *Middelburg*. This was done after the Synod had declared them all guilty of refusing to obey the synodal decrees regarding the retraction of the aforementioned accusation. This proceeding was condemned in silence by all upright people—except perhaps those who, out of ignorance or habit, worshiped the power of the Synod as if it were another Pope—and was publicly condemned with loathing by some; yet almost no one opposed it as emphatically as should have been done.

Only the single city of *Veere*, near *Middelburg*, had the courage to declare this shameless judgment void through their actions. ### Section Seven.

->Concerning my settlement in Amsterdam, and my closer connection with the purer Church forming there. Along with various special circumstances that occurred regarding its first gathering in that place.<-

A <term>Schöffe</term><note>A high-ranking municipal official or magistrate</note> of the city, who lived near us, was returning home from the countryside at about eight o'clock. No sooner did he see this unbridled behavior of such a numerous <term>Pöbel</term><note>The common people or "rabble"; used here with a tone of aristocratic or religious disdain</note>, than he, full of anxiety regarding the dangerous consequences that might arise from it, came to Labadie. He quite kindly reproached him for his far too great composure and promised him speedy assistance. He then went out and sought to calm the mob through his authority and rational arguments; but when all his exhortations achieved nothing with the "many-headed monster," he immediately had the mayors, the judge, and others called together. He pointed out to them the danger that threatened not only our house but also others; for he knew that <insert>among the mob</insert> there was neither reason nor truth—a maxim of a pagan moralist <note>likely referring to Seneca or Horace's descriptions of the fickle crowd</note> which now perfectly suited these so-called Christians as well.

## Section Eight.

### Concerning our departure from Amsterdam for Herford, our arrival there, our stay in that place, and our removal to the Princess's country estate.

Regarding our departure from Amsterdam and our journey to Herford, I will only briefly note that we were accompanied to the ship—which awaited us outside the harbor—in another vessel by many friends of our society. These came partly from Amsterdam and partly from other places; most of them, but especially some leaders of other congregations, persuaded us at our parting, indeed earnestly promised us, that they would soon follow after us. With what success they did so, I shall relate in another place, where I intend to speak more extensively concerning the renunciation of all creatures. <note>The "renunciation of all creatures" is a mystical term referring to the detachment from worldly ties and human relationships to focus solely on God.</note> Regarding the journey itself, I will add that for all of us who were traveling together—

<meta>The previous page concluded with a discussion of the impact of these speakers on their audience; this page continues that comparison between their inspired speech and the artificiality of others.</meta>

...were. And how could it have been otherwise, since the audience was bound to notice the admirable abundance of divine truths in their speeches, and the inexhaustible treasures which they brought forth from their hearts on every occasion and right on the spot, without any preparation or human study; whereas they saw others drawing their dry lectures with much effort and labor merely from their brains or from books, elaborating them artificially, and then reciting them mechanically without nature or truth. These speakers, however, even when they dealt with the oldest and most commonplace truths, always knew how to illuminate them, as it were, through a new light, and yet to present them no less clearly than naturally, without any artifice. Those who were thus instructed began to earnestly deny themselves and to completely put to death the "old man" <note>A biblical reference to the sinful nature of humanity before spiritual rebirth.</note>; and they believed with all their heart that they must first die to themselves before they could rise again with Christ. Meanwhile, our leaders never spent their intervening time in idleness, as they partly performed their other pastoral duties <term>Pastoralgeschäfte: the day-to-day spiritual care and administrative tasks of a minister</term>, and partly composed such writings that could either serve our church for its private edification, or convince the public of the authenticity and purity of our doctrine. These writings could demonstrate, in part, the innocence of our church against its slanderers, and in part, its distinction from others who deviate from us in their opinions or their conduct. Of the first kind were those which irrefutably yet modestly set forth the purity of our doctrine, its fairness in church government <term>Kirchenregiment: the system of laws and administration governing a religious body</term>, and its holiness in life. It seemed necessary to stop the mouths of the enemies of truth once and for all. While all this proceeded quite peacefully in regard to the citizens of Herford, the snake was lurking in the grass. Namely, the Magistrate (who knew as little of our condition and our doctrine as the clergy did, and without doubt did not wish to know them either) unexpectedly brought a complaint before the Imperial Chamber Court <term>Imperial Chamber Court: The highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire</term>. Church; specifically because she had brought a <term>religious sect</term><note>The term "sect" was used legally here to denote a group not officially recognized by the Peace of Westphalia.</note> into the Imperial territory that was neither Catholic, nor Lutheran, nor—as these deluded people expressed it—"Reformed." While the Princess undertook a journey to the Berlin Court, our community meanwhile withdrew for the most part to her country estate located near Herford. There, through the contemplation of the wondrous works of God and constant, highly spiritual and divine religious exercises, we gained exceptionally in the knowledge of the purest truths and the practice of the most inward piety. However, after we had lived here for several months in relative peace, the tranquility of these regions—and thus our own—was disturbed by rumors of war. These grew so prevalent daily that they soon became a clear warning for us to think seriously about our departure from these regions.

Since we had already waited a long time in vain for the Princess's <note>Princess Elisabeth of the Palatinate, who protected the Labadists at Herford</note> return from that court, and we could now no longer entertain the slightest hope of seeing divine grace and the Kingdom of Christ manifested in this land—which has proven so ungrateful toward His peaceful servants and their beneficial preaching of His pure Gospel—and since no bonds whatever forced us to await the arrival of the enemy: we therefore announced our resolution to the Princess in a collective letter. In it, we expressed our gratitude for the protection shown to us during our stay there, cited the reasons for our journey, and at the same time bid farewell to her, and soon thereafter to all of Westphalia.

Experience had taught us that God had chosen this place to purify our church of all those who, at Amsterdam, might have attempted to combine God and the world, Christ and Belial <note>A biblical figure representing lawlessness or the devil</note>, or God and Mammon <note>A term for wealth or material greed</note>, and everything else incompatible with God. regarding present and future goods and evils, I surrendered myself to Him, as if anew, more unrestrictedly and with purer faith and love than ever before. He, who as the only necessary being <note>The "necessary being" (ens necessarium) is a philosophical term for a being that must exist by its own nature and cannot not exist.</note>, also alone deserves to be blessed; just as He alone is good, as His Son testifies—He who alone truly and perfectly knows the Father, along with those to whom He wishes to reveal the Father and Himself. I wish for nothing else, therefore, than that I may be what God wills that I should be, and that He may be glorified in the manner that He wills. In a word, this renewal of my condition is to me, in a sense, a second birth of my spiritual life, the effects of which I am better able to feel than to express, and of which I perhaps have still more to expect from this same renewing and strengthening grace, until I shall finally be born into heavenly perfection and glory.

But if I am also to take into account the external circumstances in which I find myself with this **Community of God** <note>original: "Gemeine Gottes"; likely referring to the Labadist community, a pietist group seeking a return to early Christian simplicity</note>, I live here, for one, regarding my place of residence, in deep peace and great tranquility; something which **Utrecht**, amidst warriors and weapons, can perhaps hardly boast of, even among the believers. At Christmas, as a token of gratitude for their official duties <note>referring to the local parish clergy's services</note>, a voluntary tax was to be paid. Our preacher Yvon <note>Pierre Yvon (1646–1707), a leader of the Labadist community</note> gave him a free and resolute answer: that our conscience did not allow us to obey such an ordinance. For since our church perceived that this glorious instrument <note>original: "Werkzeug"; a common Pietist term for a person chosen by God to perform a specific task.</note>, chosen for the execution of such a beautiful and difficult work, was granted to her from heaven, she has surrendered herself to him as an ambassador of Christ and a discerning and faithful shepherd. She was soon convinced by experience that he walks entirely in Christ’s footsteps and is guided by His Spirit; whereby, through God’s special grace, the church has easily and happily grown into a body that appears to have only one heart and one soul <note>A reference to Acts 4:32: "All the believers were one in heart and mind."</note>.

## Second Section.

### Relates various things that occurred there from that time until our departure from Altona.

It is not part of my purpose to list in order and individually everything that our church encountered, whether adverse and to be warded off, or joyful and advantageous. One matter, however, which caused various rumors in its current state, I cannot entirely pass over in silence here. A certain Johann von Rothe <note>Johann von Rothe (1628–1710) was a prophetic figure and mystic who claimed to have divine visions; he was a controversial figure in the radical pietist circles of the 17th century.</note>, who is well enough known in these regions—a man who allowed himself to be entirely governed by his chimerical imaginings—sought through his friends to draw our congregation <term>Gemeine: the local community of believers or congregation</term> over to his side. But when he found that we preferred the common gifts of divine grace—namely, living repentance, the denial of our corrupted reason and disordered self-love, Christian faith, and Christian love—above even the true gift of prophecy (according to the Apostle *)), let alone uncertain visions and prophecies, he publicly summoned our leaders three times in succession to appear on a certain day at a place designated by him near Hamburg, where they were to call upon God together with him

God has given something so very precious, that they could return it to the Giver with a grateful heart. We all experience this same thing as often as God takes one of our members to Himself: for we are all **one body in Christ, but individually members one of another** <note>original: "Leib in Christo... des andern Glied"</note> *), as the Apostle says of true believers, the members of the genuine Church of Christ. Certainly, it must be painful when a foot, or an arm, or a finger is cut off from someone. But since the whole body is consecrated to Christ and united with Him, it is far from us that we should wish to keep any part of it as belonging to us against the will of the Head; especially since it is the well-being and desire of all to be united with their Head as closely as possible. However, we experience daily that in this, flesh and blood <note>A biblical idiom referring to human nature or kinship</note> can achieve nothing, since it is not the proximity of blood-relation that determines the measure of our love, but the fellowship of Christ; and thus, the one who is dearest to us all is the one in whom His grace reveals itself most fully.

### Section Three.

#### Concerning our departure for Friesland, and that which further befell our church there; together with some reflections upon Christian faith and love.

Although we ourselves were not thinking at all of changing our place of residence, there were nevertheless several distinguished friends in Holland who—fearing the imminent war between the Kings of Denmark and Sweden, not merely from rumors but from insight into political affairs—were concerned on our behalf; and they therefore advised us to look about for a secure place of refuge in good time. Several times the now-perfected servant of Christ, de Labadie <note>Jean de Labadie (1610–1674), the founder of the Labadist movement and a former Jesuit who became a Pietist leader.</note>, had told us that the war was always still before him, or that he had fled before the war; and we also, since we have been united with him, became partakers of this special grace of God; so that we, called to the Prince of Peace, might also enjoy His manifold peace. I, however, consider myself especially bound to acknowledge and praise the mercy of God shown to me here with a grateful soul: namely, that He so graciously led me out of Utrecht—which, as it seemed, was intended for my permanent residence—before it was seized by the flames of war,

Their principle is that man cannot love God unless he knows that God loves him and desires his salvation. But here, one must distinguish between man's duty and his power or ability to fulfill that duty. To be sure, man certainly cannot love God unless God has first loved him; nevertheless, he is bound by duty to love Him, even if God did not love him. Otherwise, the Devil would not be sinning by not loving God; for God does not love him <margin>15)</margin>. Yet he does sin, and is obligated to love God, since the fundamental reason—which binds every angelic and human creature to love God with all their heart through an indissoluble bond—is that He is always God and infinitely worthy of love, regardless of what He may do or not do, will or not will. <meta>The previous page concluded with a discussion on the nature of divine love; this page continues the exploration of God as the sole foundation of that love.</meta>

Whether we contemplate God in his essence and persons, or in his will and effects, he is and remains always the actual foundation of that pure love <note>The author refers to "Pure Love" (Amour Pur), a central concept in 17th-century mysticism regarding love for God without self-interest.</note> with which the believer loves his God. Certainly, he will love the love with which God loves him; and how could he do otherwise, since this love is nothing else than the loving God himself? But if this love could be separated from God, it would immediately cease to be the foundation, and would not even be the motivating cause <term>Bewegursache: the underlying reason or impulse that moves the soul to action</term> of his love. This love would then concentrate itself entirely in God alone, and he himself would direct the scattered parts of his soul toward their proper object, and forsake everything that was separated from his God. Nor would he thereby lose the slightest bit, not even a tiny spark, of his heavenly flame. God, who ignites and produces it—not only through what he does outside of himself, but primarily through what he is in himself (as essential love, loveliness itself, and the source of love)—would always support, animate, and preserve this pure love. His gifts, therefore, are never actually the cause of love, even when they are given to assist it. Its unquenchable fire is nourished by the all-sufficient God himself, who alone is pure love and who fully satisfies it. By no means, however, does the soul undervalue any particular motivating cause that God gives it, much less should it reject the same. Rather, all such causes give it great joy, because it [finds] in them

Behold there the rules, or rather the characteristics, of the pure love of God, from which it can be gathered how holily a faithful soul, purely loving God, receives and uses everything, and how she embraces nothing other than God Himself in all her relationships with Him and in the goods with which He gifts her.

Self-love <note>German: *Eigenliebe*; in this context, it refers to a disordered, selfish love that places the self above the Creator</note> does exactly the opposite: it makes God subservient to itself and makes itself its own final and only goal—indeed, as much as it is able, it even attempts to make itself the goal of God Himself. This is the same as if it wished to make itself the God of God Himself. It is therefore the worst of all forms of idolatry <term>Abgötterey: the worship of false idols or the self</term> and the highest of all impieties. It loves God and Christ no further than for its own sake, and in all those bonds of divine goodness and charity, it seeks nothing but itself. 

If, for example, a selfish person loves—or appears to love—God because God is doing him good, he is in truth loving nothing but himself. He does not love God and His love because of their inner worthiness of being loved, but because they serve his own advantage and well-being, should he be able to partake of them. Were this not the case, God and His love would no longer seem lovely to him, and he would neither be able nor willing to love them. Thus, selfishness <note>German: *Eigensucht*; a more pathological or addictive form of self-interest</note> loves God’s blessings for their pleasantness, their splendor, and their utility; without these, it would care little for them. 

Every natural man <note>The "natural man" refers to a person living according to worldly instincts rather than spiritual grace</note> finds this hateful and contemptible when such self-love has physical things as its object; yet it is indisputably much more hateful when it extends itself to the spiritual blessings of the soul. It is all the more dangerous because, under the appearance of a spiritual love, it is nevertheless entirely carnal <note>German: *fleischlich*; pertaining to the lower, unredeemed nature of man</note>. Through pure love <term>reine Liebe: disinterested love for God, seeking nothing in return</term>, however, the living faith of a sou—

to heap upon them insults and slanders.

The sole reason for this most unjust accusation seems to be that our people do not—as those others are accustomed to do—urge men to be assured of their salvation before they have seriously considered **self-denial** <term>Selbstverleugnung: the act of putting aside one's own will to follow God's will</term> and the **service of God**, and have consecrated themselves entirely to Him. Nor do we insist they must know they are numbered among the **elect** <term>Auserwählten: those chosen by God for salvation</term>, that Christ died for them specifically, and that they are reconciled with God through his blood. Furthermore, we do not link the power of the blood of Christ to cleanse us from **sins** to the direct and actual thought which arises in us after a sin has been committed—namely, that the blood of Christ was shed for our sins, and especially for this most recent one—even if such a thought arises when God wills it and works through His Spirit. 

Now, as far as the first part of this doctrine is concerned, we not only admit that we do not teach it, but we also publicly maintain that it is highly false, that it dishonors God and Christ, and moreover, that it leads souls to destruction. The cause of this doctrine is nothing other than that imperfect, indeed erroneous, concept of **saving faith** <term>seligmachender Glaube: the specific type of faith required for eternal salvation</term>, where it is held to be a certain persuasion and confidence that one is elected, given by the Father to the Son, purchased by the blood of the Son, and reconciled with God through his death, which has satisfied **divine justice**. <note>The author is critiquing a version of Calvinist or Lutheran assurance that prioritizes a mental conviction of being "chosen" over the actual practice of a holy life.</note>

# The External Cross and the True Church

The external cross, when it must be, and when God lays it upon them in order to faithfully correspond to their calling, to the truth itself, and to the Spirit of the Lord, is to be taken up honestly and with one's whole heart; and the paths that He prepares for them—be they of shame or of pain, or of the hatred and persecution of men, or of exile, or of imprisonment, or of death itself—are to be trodden willingly and steadfastly. For whoever loves his life, let alone what is less than life, more than Christ, is not worthy of Him <note>A reference to Matthew 10:37-38, a central tenet for radical reformation groups regarding martyrdom and devotion.</note>. In short, this is the distinguishing mark of the Christian: that he is not only ready for all of this, but also in deed willingly suffers and takes it upon himself. Rather than being hindered or frightened away, he allows himself to be further strengthened and driven forward in the ways that he had previously recognized through the light of truth and the divine Word.

These are the three parts in which, in our opinion, the cross of Christ <term>Cross of Christ: here used not just as the wooden crucifix, but as the sum of all spiritual and physical suffering endured for faith</term> generally consists; and we would not believe ourselves to be a true church of Christ if God, according to His fatherly mercy toward us, had not also made the members of the same partakers of this threefold grace. As far as the first part is concerned, it is sufficiently clear from what I have just said about the **inner cross** <note>The "inner cross" refers to the internal struggle against sin and the ego, as opposed to "external" persecution.</note> that we bear it earnestly and in deed. As for the second, namely the willingness to [bear] the ex-

Regarding the third point, however, one must diligently close their eyes not to see how, in the midst of the ways of the cross—and indeed the most manifold cross—this church was planted and established. I would be careful to mention even the slightest bit of this, lest it seem I am acting like those who, on every occasion and even without necessity, boast so much of their sufferings, unmindful that someone could let their body be burned and yet be empty of the genuine and pure love of God; and thus have no part at all in the true cross of Christ. But since these very people, who make common cause with those standing in the reputation of the clergy, force us to a certain extent to bear witness to the truth in this matter—just as their kind formerly forced the Apostle—we make no matter of conscience, following his example, to boast to a certain extent of the cross of Christ, and to praise God the Father that he has adorned us, and still adorns us, with the marks of honor <note>original: "Ehrenzeichen" – likely referring to the "stigmata" or spiritual marks of suffering</note> of his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

And I hardly believe that any other servant of Christ <note>original: "Diener Christi"</note> in our times has experienced so much hatred and persecution from worldly-minded and malicious men, as they did not cease to hunt him—as David says of himself—like a partridge through mountain and valley. I was an eyewitness to some of the storms which were stirred up by the enemies of this Reformation <note>original: "Kirchenverbesserung," literally "church improvement"</note> in Zeeland and afterwards in Amsterdam, some of which I also touched upon in the first part of this work: and here I can also include the slanders—no less abominable and devilish than they were tasteless and ridiculous—which countless tongues, inflamed by hell, spread everywhere against the servant of God and this emerging Church of Christ, and which some embittered enemies of the same and of genuine piety did not hesitate to confirm through libelous writings. This Cross of Christ <note>original: "Kreuz Christi"</note> then—namely, the contradiction from sinners—we had to take upon ourselves, and disregard the shame, following the example of our Savior, who for that very reason called his own blessed, and commanded them to be joyful and of good cheer.

I wish to add nothing further than the praise and glory of my heavenly Father, that he has also granted me a particular portion of this cross—partly through slanders and insults, partly through bodily pains, not to mention the internal sufferings here—and that he has simultaneously given me the disposition to take it upon myself and bear it with a joyful spirit and not unwillingly. For it is the effect of his paternal and divine goodness that he pours the lovely oil of his adored will so abundantly over even the hardest cross, which he occasionally lays upon his own, that its thorns or nails seem to lose their stings immediately. To his honor, therefore, I can testify that, strengthened by his power, I have often kissed his hand with a willing heart when he sent me either the pains of the stone <note>likely kidney or bladder stones, a common and agonizing ailment in the 17th century</note>, which I first suffered in Westphalia and afterwards often in Altona, or the gout, which already tormented me there and still fetters me so greatly to my bed or my chair that I have not stepped upon the ground for almost two years. Truly, the pure love of the divine will is sufficient for the children of God to transform the nature of things, because it makes even the bitterest thing sweet to them when they see that the highest honor of God is thereby promoted in the execution of his divine decree. ## Fourth Section.

### Concerning the Causes of our Disagreement with Doctor Voetius. Conclusion.

Among the wondrous ways of God, I believe I must especially mention here those by which He uses the erroneous actions and speeches not only of the wicked, but also of the good, in such a way that others are thereby led to the truth and strengthened within it. We have experienced this often and in many ways since God began the work of gathering this, His church, among us; of which I will now cite a fairly well-known example that particularly fits my current purpose. I mean that the venerable Doctor and Professor of Theology, Gisbert Voetius <note>Gisbert Voetius (1589–1676) was a highly influential Dutch Reformed theologian and a leading opponent of the Labadist movement</note>, famous for his great and multifaceted learning, opposed this work of God through public theses <note>original: "Theses" — formal academic propositions for debate</note> at its very origin. He prejudiced many against it, but especially paved the way and opened the mouths of students of all kinds and from all lands to speak boldly against our institution <note>The author refers to the "house-church" or communal society established by Jean de Labadie</note>, to criticize it according to each person's own mind and pleasure, and to spread the sentence of condemnation against it everywhere, since it had such a great theologian on its side! To confess the truth, this caused me no small grief at first: however, I soon learned that, in such a matter, one must leave everything to God, who can call forth light even out of the darkness, and who is often accustomed to give things a completely different outcome than we had judged. Not a few people, I believe, were deterred from a serious and free investigation into the true nature of the matter by the mere authority of such a great man <note>Likely referring to a high-ranking theologian or academic official whose reputation lent weight to his criticisms</note>: yet we have also since experienced with the greatest certainty that, conversely, these very theses taught others that the path they were attacking was the correct and secure one, and gave them cause to research the truth more precisely.

But since these theses, which were only distributed in an academic fashion, could be viewed as fleeting, temporary pamphlets, I had no desire to renew this pain by contesting them; however, I found myself compelled to change my resolution when I saw, among others, those which refer to my *Eucleria* <note>original: "Euklerie"; referring to the author's autobiographical work 'Eucleria', which defends his religious views</note> reprinted anew and inserted into the final volume of his *Ecclesiastical Policy* <note>original: "Kirchen-Polizey"; a term for the administration and legal regulation of the church</note>. For I believed it would not be improper if I presented my opinion—lovingly, amicably, and modestly—to this man, who for many years has been my dear friend, regarding what he judges there partly dogmatically <note>concerning established church doctrine</note> and partly historically about our conduct; because I knew these things better than he, since I myself took part in them—

2) Can a congregation <note>original: "Gemeine," a term often used by Pietists to denote a community of believers rather than just a formal parish</note> consisting of mere worldly people <note>original: "Weltmenschen," referring to those who live according to secular values rather than spiritual ones</note> be regarded as a true, particular Church of Christ, or as His body and a part of His universal and mystical body, simply because it calls itself Christian and Reformed?

---

Thus far the female author, who survived the completion of this writing by only a few days. She died in 1678, in the 72nd year of her age, from a violent attack of the stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note> and gout. From two letters—one to Princess Elisabeth <note>Elisabeth of the Palatinate, a noted philosopher and friend of Schurman</note> and one to certain unnamed friends of Schurman, which the editor of the original, presumably *Yvon* or *Dulignon*, has appended—one sees that her end was like her life: full of inward surrender to the will of God, full of praise and glory to God amidst the most violent pains until the final moment, full of longing for her redemption and joyful certainty of eternal life. Since these letters contain nothing else of note, they may conveniently remain untranslated; as may some other letters found among her papers after her death, which are appended to the Latin original, to which we refer any interested readers so as not to unnecessarily expand this little work.
